system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2124-04-12 15:03:00 to 2124-04-15 14:59:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with advanced HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, and a tracheostomy was admitted after accidentally dislodging his GJ tube at his nursing home. He was unable to take his morning medications and was found to have leukocytosis and tachycardia. He received IV fluids and a dose of metoprolol, which resolved his tachycardia. A temporary Foley catheter was placed to maintain the gastrostomy tract, and the GJ tube was successfully replaced the following day under fluoroscopic guidance. His leukocytosis improved without antibiotics, and urine culture showed mixed flora consistent with colonization rather than infection. He remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Chronic issues including HIV, seizures, COPD, and abdominal pain were managed with his home medications. The decision was made to remove his chronic indwelling Foley catheter as an outpatient due to infection risk. He was discharged back to extended care after a two-day stay.
problems: Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
Other dependence on machines, supplemental oxygen

microbiology.comments: HIV-1 RNA detected, less than 20 copies/mL.  Performed using the ___ HIV-1 Test v2.0.  Detection Range: 20-10,000,000 copies/mL.  This test is approved for monitoring HIV-1 viral load in known HIV-positive patients. It is not approved for diagnosis of acute HIV infection.  In symptomatic acute HIV infection (acute retroviral syndrome), the viral load is usually very high (>>1000 copies/mL). If acute HIV infection is clinically suspected and there is a detectable but low viral load, please contact the laboratory for interpretation.  It is recommended that any NEW positive HIV-1 viral load result, in the absence of positive serology, be confirmed by submitting a new sample FOR HIV-1 PCR, in addition to serological testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You were brought in because you had a fever at the nursing home. Can you tell me how you’re feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever’s gone down, but I feel weak. They said my heart was racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart rate was high when you arrived. We gave you fluids, and it’s improved. We’re checking your urine and blood because we think the fever might be from a urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a catheter before, but they took it out yesterday. I’ve been peeing on my own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But sometimes infections can still happen after removal. Your urine test showed signs of infection, so we started antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you vancomycin and levofloxacin at first. But we’ll adjust based on the culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds already. Will this affect them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reviewing all your medications. You’re still getting your HIV meds, seizure meds, and breathing treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to miss those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray. It shows some fluid in the lungs, but no pneumonia. It might be related to your chronic lung disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had breathing problems for years. I need suctioning a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping your trach mask on and giving albuterol as needed. We’ll keep an eye on your oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back. You have Pseudomonas and Enterococcus. These can be serious, so we’re switching your antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are those resistant bugs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pseudomonas can be tough, but your tests show it’s sensitive to cefepime. Enterococcus is being treated with linezolid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, cefepime will be IV. We’ll place a PICC line so you can get it at home. Linezolid is oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About two weeks total. You’ll finish the course at the nursing home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still getting Truvada, darunavir, and ritonavir daily. Your latest viral load is undetectable, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding your citalopram for now. It can interact with linezolid and cause serotonin syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on it for anxiety. Is it safe to restart later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once you finish linezolid, you can restart it. We’ll make sure your care team knows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed the PICC line this morning. It went well. You’ll get cefepime through it every 8 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some pressure, but it shouldn’t be painful. We’ll keep it clean and check it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the linezolid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a pill you’ll take twice a day. We’ll monitor your blood count in a week to watch for any side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any other changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on metoprolol for your fast heart rate. We recommend you follow up with a heart specialist about your SVT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for years. They said it might need ablation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s something to discuss with electrophysiology. We’ll send a note to your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’ve been fever-free, and your white count is coming down. We’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to the nursing home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’ll continue both antibiotics there. The PICC line will be removed after your last dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your regular medications are listed, including your HIV, seizure, and breathing meds. Restart citalopram after linezolid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your sister and care team get a full update. Call if you develop fever or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with advanced HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, and a tracheostomy was admitted from his nursing facility with fever and tachycardia. Initial evaluation revealed leukocytosis and a urinalysis positive for nitrites and white blood cells. A chest X-ray showed increased interstitial markings without pneumonia. Urine culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterococcus species, leading to a diagnosis of urinary tract infection with sepsis. He was treated with cefepime and linezolid after a PICC line was placed. His condition improved, and he remained afebrile. Chronic conditions including HIV, seizures, COPD, and abdominal pain were managed with home medications. Citalopram was held due to interaction risk with linezolid. He was discharged back to extended care with plans to complete a two-week course of IV and oral antibiotics and follow up on his SVT and medication reconciliation.
